lead: The Domain Name System (DNS) turns the human‑friendly names we type, like www.irctc.co.in, into the numeric IP addresses that routers need. It exists because remembering numbers is hard and because IP addresses can change while names stay the same. DNS is used by every web browser, email client, and mobile app that accesses the Internet.
prereq: You need: IP addressing from Chapter 2 and the basics of sockets from socket‑programming with TCP and UDP.

blocks.text: DNS is organized as a tree that starts at the root servers. The root points to top‑level domain (TLD) servers such as .com, .in, .org. Each TLD delegates authority to second‑level domains (e.g., irctc.co.in). A zone is the part of the name space for which a server holds authoritative records. The root zone, the .in zone, and the irctc.co.in zone are examples.

items: Root zone – managed by a set of globally distributed root servers.
TLD zone – managed by the registry for that TLD (e.g., .in).
Second‑level zone – managed by the domain owner (e.g., irctc.co.in).

blocks.where: remaining_TTL is the time left before a cached record expires; TTL is the Time‑to‑Live value set by the authoritative server; elapsed is the time already spent since the record was cached.

blocks.text: A DNS response contains resource records (RR). The most common RR types are A (IPv4 address), CNAME (canonical name alias), MX (mail exchange server), and NS (name server). When a client asks for www.irctc.co.in, it typically sends a recursive query to its local resolver.

items: Resolver checks its cache. If a valid record exists, it returns it.
If not, the resolver sends an iterative query to a root server.
Root returns the NS records for the .in TLD.
Resolver queries a .in server, which returns NS records for irctc.co.in.
Resolver finally queries an irctc.co.in authoritative server, which returns the A record.
Recursive query – client asks resolver to do all the work and return the final answer.
Iterative query – resolver asks one server at a time and follows referrals.

blocks.text: Resolvers cache answers to reduce traffic and latency. Each record carries a TTL in seconds. While the TTL has not expired, the cached copy is used; after expiration the resolver must fetch a fresh copy.

items: Typical TTL values: 300 s for dynamic records, 86400 s (24 h) for static records.
Cache size is limited; least‑recently‑used entries are evicted first.

blocks.text: DNS uses UDP port 53 for most queries because it is fast and fits in a single packet. If the answer does not fit (e.g., DNSSEC or many records), the server sets the TC (truncated) flag and the client retries over TCP port 53.
Only a few universities teach dynamic update, where a client can add, delete, or modify records in a zone using the UPDATE operation over TCP with authentication.

examples.question: You are in Chennai and need to open https://www.irctc.co.in. The local recursive resolver has an empty cache. Each DNS query to any server takes 30 ms (round‑trip). Show the steps the resolver follows, list the IP address obtained, and compute the total time taken for the lookup.
steps: Step 1 – Query a root server (30 ms). The root returns NS records for the .in TLD.
Step 2 – Query a .in TLD server (30 ms, cumulative 60 ms). The TLD returns NS records for the irctc.co.in zone.
Step 3 – Query an irctc.co.in authoritative server (30 ms, cumulative 90 ms). The server returns the A record 203.197.0.1 for www.irctc.co.in.
examples.answer: The resolver obtains IP address 203.197.0.1 and the total lookup time is 90 ms.

traps: Confusing an authoritative name server with a recursive resolver; the former only answers for its own zone, the latter performs the whole lookup.
Assuming DNS always uses TCP; most queries use UDP unless the response is too large.
Treating the TTL as a fixed global value; each record carries its own TTL and the remaining time depends on when it was cached.
Thinking that a CNAME record replaces the original name; the client must still follow the CNAME to the final A record.
Believing that a cache entry is removed immediately after TTL expires; many resolvers keep the stale entry until a new query is made.

quiz.q: Which UDP/TCP port number does DNS use?
Explain the difference between a recursive query and an iterative query.
quiz.a: In a recursive query the resolver does all the steps and returns the final answer; in an iterative query the resolver asks one server, receives a referral, and must query the next server itself.

quiz.q: If a cached A record has TTL = 600 s and was stored 200 s ago, how many seconds remain before it expires?
A DNS response contains 2 A records and 1 MX record. The total size is 512 bytes. Will the client need to retry over TCP? Justify.
quiz.a: No. The UDP limit is 512 bytes for classic DNS. Since the response fits, the client will not switch to TCP.

quiz.q: During a heavy traffic period, a resolver receives many queries for the same domain. Explain how caching reduces load on authoritative servers and improves response time.
quiz.a: When the first query is answered, the resolver stores the records with their TTL. Subsequent queries within the TTL are answered from the cache, so no additional messages travel to the authoritative servers, reducing network traffic and latency.

quiz.q: A DNS response is truncated (TC flag set). What steps does the client take and why?
quiz.a: The client re‑issues the same query over TCP port 53. TCP can carry larger messages, allowing the full answer (often needed for DNSSEC or many records).

beyond: Not for the exam. DNS is moving toward DNS over HTTPS (DoH) and DNS over TLS (DoT) to protect privacy. Large cloud providers run anycast DNS services that answer from the nearest data center, reducing latency. Researchers explore DNS-based load balancing and service discovery for IoT devices. To learn more, search for "DoH implementation" and "DNSSEC deployment".
